```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)
source("src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")
R3 <- "results/study3"
rd <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(R3, f), show_col_types = FALSE)
both <- function(stem) bind_rows(wi = rd(paste0(stem, "_wi.csv")), fce = rd(paste0(stem, "_fce.csv")), .id = "corpus")
js <- function(f) fromJSON(file.path(R3, f))
TH <- js("threshold.json")
CK <- list(wi = js("decompose_wi.json"), fce = js("decompose_fce.json"))
AL <- list(wi = js("align_wi.json"), fce = js("align_fce.json"))
SP <- list(wi = js("spill_wi.json"), fce = js("spill_fce.json"))
s4 <- both("split4")
m4 <- both("split4_means")
sh <- both("shares")
rc <- both("rate_cost")
dec <- both("spill_decay")
ca <- rd("clean_assoc.csv")
inc <- rd("increment.csv")
cf <- rd("coefs.csv")
cl <- both("classic")
cal <- rd("calibration.csv")
calc <- rd("calibration_contrasts.csv")
CORP <- c(wi = "W&I", fce = "FCE")
BUCKETS <- c("mechanical", "function word", "content-word choice", "multi-word / order")

f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
r0 <- function(x, d = 0) round(x, d) + 0  # no negative zero
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", r0(100 * x))
pci <- function(v, lo, hi) sprintf("%.0f [%.0f, %.0f]", r0(100 * v), r0(100 * lo), r0(100 * hi))
ci2 <- function(v, lo, hi, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f [%.", d, "f, %.", d, "f]"), r0(v, d), r0(lo, d), r0(hi, d))
S4 <- function(c, p, m = "mean_surprisal") filter(s4, corpus == c, measure == m, part == p)
M4 <- function(c, g, p, m = "mean_surprisal") filter(m4, corpus == c, measure == m, group == g)[[p]]
SH <- function(c, col, cut = "bucket") filter(sh, corpus == c, cut == !!cut, col == !!col)
RC <- function(c, cat, comp = "total", cut = "bucket") filter(rc, corpus == c, cut == !!cut, cat == !!cat, comp == !!comp)
INC <- function(c, m) filter(inc, corpus == c, model == m)
CL <- function(c, m, s) filter(cl, corpus == c, measure == m, stat == s)
CAL <- function(g) filter(cal, group == g)
corr_part <- function(c, g) M4(c, g, "omission") + M4(c, g, "context") + M4(c, g, "error_tokens")
```

# 1. Introduction

Studies 1 and 2 showed that the mean surprisal of an essay under a small
language model (OLMo-2 1B, 8-subword window) tracks writing proficiency.
Study 3 asks what that signal is made of. The proposal posed three questions.

- **RQ1.** Does the surprisal of learner writing decompose into interpretable
  components?
- **RQ2.** Are the components differentially associated with proficiency?
- **RQ3.** Do the components carry information beyond simpler measures? The
  simpler measure here is the count of errors that a human annotator marked.

A component is defined counterfactually. It is the part of an essay's
surprisal that would disappear if a given kind of error were corrected. Two
learner corpora with expert corrections supply the counterfactual. Each essay
is corrected, the corrected essay is scored with the same instrument, and the
difference between the two versions is split exactly over the corrections and
their ERRANT error types. What remains, the surprisal of the writer's own
words in the corrected essay, is the *clean* part. Because the parts add up to
the essay's mean surprisal, their covariances with proficiency add up too, so
the proficiency signal splits exactly over the components.

The proposal's δ-vector method, and why it describes words rather than
errors, is reported in the appendix (`appendix/appendix.qmd`).

# 3. Method

## 3.1 Corpora

**W&I+LOCNESS** is the BEA-2019 release of the Cambridge English Write &
Improve corpus with the LOCNESS essays (Yannakoudakis et al. 2018; Bryant et
al. 2019; LOCNESS
courtesy of the Centre for English Corpus Linguistics, Université catholique
de Louvain). It holds `r format(CK$wi$n_units, big.mark = ",")` learner essays
at CEFR levels A (`r format(CK$wi$n_by_group$A, big.mark = ",")`), B
(`r format(CK$wi$n_by_group$B, big.mark = ",")`) and C
(`r CK$wi$n_by_group$C`), and `r CK$wi$n_by_group$N` essays by native student
writers (LOCNESS, level N). The criterion is the CEFR level (A = 1, B = 2,
C = 3). LOCNESS has no criterion and is described separately. W&I+LOCNESS is
the main corpus.

**FCE** is the BEA-2019 release of the First Certificate in English exam
scripts (Yannakoudakis, Briscoe & Medlock 2011). Each script holds two
answers. The unit is the script, with both answers pooled, and the criterion
is the script score (1–40). The one script scored 0 is left out, which leaves
`r format(CK$fce$n_units, big.mark = ",")` scripts. FCE is the replication.

Both corpora are used with the first annotator's corrections:
`r format(CK$wi$n_corrections, big.mark = ",")` corrections in the W&I learner
essays and `r format(CK$fce$n_corrections, big.mark = ",")` in FCE, plus
`r format(CK$wi$n_flagged, big.mark = ",")` and
`r format(CK$fce$n_flagged, big.mark = ",")` spans that the annotator flagged
without correcting. Both corpora are licensed for research without
redistribution, so no learner text is quoted.

## 3.2 Instrument

Surprisal is computed exactly as in Study 1. Each spaCy token is scored by
the surprisal (bits) of its first subword under OLMo-2 1B base, given the 8
subwords that end at that subword. An essay's mean surprisal is the mean over
its scored tokens. The high-token rate counts tokens above τ =
`r sprintf("%.2f", TH$tau_bits)` bits, the 90th percentile of token surprisal
in the strongest third of the ELLIPSE development essays.

## 3.3 Corrections and error types

The gold edits are character spans with a replacement. Applying all of an
essay's corrections gives the corrected essay. Whitespace is repaired locally
where an edit meets the surrounding text, and flagged spans stay as written.
The corrected essays are parsed with the same spaCy pipeline and scored with
the same instrument.

Each correction takes the ERRANT type (Bryant, Felice & Briscoe 2017) of the
edit it overlaps in the released M2 files, whose tokens are walked back onto
the original characters. All but
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * CK$wi$unmapped_share)` (W&I) and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * CK$fce$unmapped_share)` (FCE) of the corrections
receive a type. The types are grouped into four kinds of correction
(Table 1), fixed before the analysis (D33). Unknown and untyped edits are
*unclassified*. Nine finer ERRANT groups (D28) are reported as a supplement.

```{r}
#| label: t-buckets
tibble(`kind of correction` = BUCKETS,
       `ERRANT categories (operation prefix dropped)` = c(
         "SPELL, ORTH, PUNCT, VERB:FORM, VERB:SVA, VERB:INFL, VERB:TENSE, NOUN:NUM, NOUN:INFL, MORPH, ADJ:FORM, CONTR, NOUN:POSS",
         "DET, PREP, PRON, CONJ, PART", "NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV", "OTHER, WO")) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 1. Kinds of correction")
```

## 3.4 Alignment

An original token is the writer's *own* when none of its characters lies in a
corrected or flagged span. An own token is *aligned* when the corrected essay
has a scored token at the mapped position with the same text.
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * AL$wi$aligned_of_own)` (W&I) and
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * AL$fce$aligned_of_own)` (FCE) of own tokens align.
As a check, aligned tokens whose 8-subword window is identical in both
versions should keep their surprisal, and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * AL$wi$same_window_abs_delta_lt_0.05)` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * AL$fce$same_window_abs_delta_lt_0.05)` of them move
by less than .05 bits (bf16 batch noise).

## 3.5 The exact split

For a unit with n scored tokens, let O be the aligned own tokens, with
surprisal s_orig in the original essay and s_corr in the corrected essay, and
let clean be the mean of s_corr over O. Then

S_orig = clean + omission + context + error tokens,

where *omission* is the sum of s_orig − s_corr over own words that directly
follow a missing word, divided by n; *context* is the same sum over the other
own words; and *error tokens* is the excess over clean of every other token
(the corrected tokens themselves). This four-part split (D24) holds exactly
for every unit. The same split is applied to the high-token rate.

The split by kind of correction refines it (D28):

S_orig = clean + Σ_c (at site_c + spill_c) + flagged + residual.

- **At site.** For a replacement or unnecessary-word correction, the excess
  over clean of the tokens it covers. For a missing-word correction, the
  surprisal change of the own word right after the gap.
- **Spill.** The surprisal change of the other own words whose window holds
  the correction. When a window holds several corrections, the change is
  split among them by Shapley values (Shapley 1953) with the correction as
  the baseline. The players are the corrections in the window, and each is
  either as written or corrected, so the values add up to the word's
  surprisal change exactly (D27). The partial versions are re-tokenised from
  the text and scored in fp32. Each word's values are shifted equally so that
  they add up to its stored change. The `r SP$wi$status$too_many` W&I words
  with more than 7 corrections in the window split the change equally.
- **Flagged.** The excess of tokens the annotator flagged without correcting.
- **Residual.** The surprisal change of own words with no correction in the
  window, and of own words that do not align. It is instrument noise.

The split holds exactly (to 10⁻⁹ bits) in every unit.

## 3.6 Statistics

Because the parts add up to S_orig, the covariance of S_orig with the
criterion is the sum of the parts' covariances. Each part's *share of the
proficiency signal* is its covariance with the criterion divided by that of
S_orig, among learners. Shares add up to 100%, can be negative, and come with
95% CIs from 2,000 unit bootstraps. Spearman ρ is reported alongside.

*Frequency and cost.* A component pooled over the units of one level is the
error rate times the mean cost per error. The difference between the lowest
and highest level (W&I A − C; FCE score 1–23 vs 32–40) splits into a rate
part and a cost part by the midpoint rule.

*The clean part.* The clean part's association with the criterion is
reported raw and as a partial Spearman correlation given the plain share of
corrected tokens (D31).

*RQ3.* The error counts B are the rate of each of the nine ERRANT groups,
the rate of flagged spans, and log n. The compact surprisal terms S are
clean, mean at-site bits per error and mean spill bits per error. Ridge
regression (imputation, scaling and the penalty fitted within folds) is
evaluated by 10 × 10-fold cross-validation stratified by level or score band,
with the same folds for every model. ΔR² compares B + S with B, with a
2,000-resample unit bootstrap of the out-of-fold predictions.

## 3.7 Calibration corpora

To place learner writing among other writing, the same instrument scores
public documents that the learner corpora's licences do not restrict:
PERSUADE 2.0 essays by US secondary-school students (Crossley et al. 2024),
split by the corpus's English-learner flag and by holistic score, and English
Wikipedia articles created in 2018–21 (in the model's training data) or in
2026 (after it). Every document, learner essays included, is cut to 200–600
words at a sentence end, and 300 documents are sampled per external group.

## 3.8 Classic measures (post hoc)

The follow-up in Section 4.5 applies the same counterfactual to the
phraseological and lexical measures of applied linguistics, computed against
the Dolma reference corpora of Study 2: bigram MI and ΔP, the share of
bigrams with MI ≥ 3, Study 2's dependency MI (amod, dobj, advmod), the mean
log frequency of content words, and Study 2's lemma frequency. Each essay is
rebuilt with every subset of its kinds of correction applied, re-parsed, and
re-measured. Exact Shapley values over the kinds of correction then split
each measure's original-minus-corrected difference.

# 4. Results

## 4.1 What surprisal is made of

```{r}
#| label: t-split4
lab <- c(wi = "W&I", fce = "FCE")
m4 |>
  filter(measure == "mean_surprisal") |>
  transmute(corpus = lab[corpus], group = recode(group, N = "N (LOCNESS)", learners = "all learners"),
            units = n_units, total, clean, omission, context, `error tokens` = error_tokens,
            `corrections` = omission + context + error_tokens) |>
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Table 2. Mean surprisal per unit (bits) and its four parts, by CEFR level (W&I) and script-score band (FCE)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-split4
#| fig-cap: "What the corrections add to mean surprisal, by level. The clean part (about 5.2–5.7 bits) is not shown"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
d <- m4 |>
  filter(measure == "mean_surprisal", group != "learners") |>
  select(corpus, group, omission, context, `error tokens` = error_tokens) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(corpus, group), names_to = "part", values_to = "bits") |>
  mutate(corpus = factor(lab[corpus], c("W&I", "FCE")),
         part = factor(part, c("error tokens", "context", "omission")))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(group, bits, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(~corpus, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`error tokens` = "#b2182b", context = "#ef8a62", omission = "#fddbc7"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "CEFR level (N = LOCNESS) / script-score band", y = "Bits added to mean surprisal") +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "split4", 8, 3.6, dir = R3)
p
```

The clean part is nearly constant. It is
`r f2(M4("wi", "A", "clean"))`, `r f2(M4("wi", "B", "clean"))` and
`r f2(M4("wi", "C", "clean"))` bits at A, B and C, and between
`r f2(min(filter(m4, corpus == "fce", measure == "mean_surprisal", group != "learners")$clean))`
and
`r f2(max(filter(m4, corpus == "fce", measure == "mean_surprisal", group != "learners")$clean))`
bits across the FCE score bands. What the corrections add falls from
`r f2(corr_part("wi", "A"))` bits at A to `r f2(corr_part("wi", "C"))` at C,
and from `r f2(corr_part("fce", "1-23"))` to `r f2(corr_part("fce", "32-40"))`
bits across the FCE bands (Figure 1). The error tokens' own excess is the
largest part. The context part, the extra surprisal of correct words that
follow an error, is about a quarter to a third of what the corrections add.
At every level, most of an essay's surprisal is the clean part, but nearly
all of the difference between levels is in the corrections.

LOCNESS has a C-level correction part (`r f2(corr_part("wi", "N"))` bits) and
a higher clean part (`r f2(M4("wi", "N", "clean"))` bits). Native minus C is
`r ci2(CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$total[1], CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$total[2], CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$total[3])`
bits in total and
`r ci2(CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$clean[1], CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$clean[2], CK$wi$native_minus_C$mean_surprisal$clean[3])`
in the clean part.

```{r}
#| label: t-calibration
glab <- c(`W&I A` = "W&I A", `W&I B` = "W&I B", `W&I C` = "W&I C", LOCNESS = "LOCNESS (native student writers)",
          `ELLIPSE <= 2.5` = "ELLIPSE, Overall ≤ 2.5", `ELLIPSE 3-3.5` = "ELLIPSE, Overall 3–3.5",
          `ELLIPSE >= 4` = "ELLIPSE, Overall ≥ 4", persuade_ell = "PERSUADE, English learners",
          persuade_native = "PERSUADE, not English learners",
          persuade_native_hi = "PERSUADE, not English learners, score ≥ 5",
          wiki_old = "Wikipedia, created 2018–21 (in training data)", wiki_new = "Wikipedia, created 2026 (after training)")
cal |>
  transmute(group = glab[group], documents = n, `mean surprisal` = mean, `95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", lo, hi), SD = sd) |>
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Table 3. Mean surprisal per document (bits), 200–600 words, cut at a sentence end")
```

Table 3 places these values among other writing. C-level learners
(`r f2(CAL("W&I C")$mean)`), the top ELLIPSE band (`r f2(CAL("ELLIPSE >= 4")$mean)`)
and US students not classified as English learners
(`r f2(CAL("persuade_native")$mean)`) fall within .03 bits of each other.
PERSUADE essays scored 5 or 6 are slightly lower
(`r f2(CAL("persuade_native_hi")$mean)`), and PERSUADE essays by English
learners are higher (`r f2(CAL("persuade_ell")$mean)`). University essays
(LOCNESS, `r f2(CAL("LOCNESS")$mean)`) and Wikipedia
(`r f2(CAL("wiki_old")$mean)`–`r f2(CAL("wiki_new")$mean)`) are *more*
surprising than the C-level essays. Wikipedia written after the model's
training data was collected is only
`r with(filter(calc, a == "wiki_new"), ci2(diff, lo, hi))` bits more
surprising than Wikipedia it was trained on, so memorisation barely moves the
statistic at this window.

Lower mean surprisal is therefore not better writing once errors are rare.
Among learners, the measure falls as errors become rarer. Above the C level,
topic, register and vocabulary set its value, and more informative or more
literate prose scores higher.

## 4.2 Components by error type

```{r}
#| label: t-bucket-cost
mn <- bind_rows(wi = read_csv(file.path(R3, "means_wi.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE),
                fce = read_csv(file.path(R3, "means_fce.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE), .id = "corpus") |>
  rename(col = 2)
rc |>
  filter(cut == "bucket", cat %in% BUCKETS) |>
  select(corpus, cat, comp, rate_all, cost_all) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = comp, values_from = cost_all) |>
  left_join(mn |> filter(str_detect(col, "\\|total$")) |> transmute(corpus, cat = str_remove(col, "\\|total$"), bits = learners),
            by = c("corpus", "cat")) |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], `kind of correction` = cat, `errors per 100 tokens` = rate_all,
            `bits per error, at site` = at_site, `bits per error, spill` = spill, `bits per error, total` = total,
            `bits added to mean surprisal` = bits) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Table 4. Frequency and cost of each kind of correction, all learners pooled. The last column is the component's mean contribution to an essay's mean surprisal")
```

Table 4 gives each component's frequency and cost. Mechanical errors
(spelling, punctuation, inflection) are the most frequent, at
`r f2(RC("wi", "mechanical")$rate_all)` per 100 tokens in W&I, and they
contribute the most surprisal. Content-word and multi-word corrections are
rarer but the costliest per error (`r f2(RC("wi", "content-word choice")$cost_all)`
and `r f2(RC("wi", "multi-word / order")$cost_all)` bits in W&I).
Function-word errors cost little at their own site
(`r f2(RC("wi", "function word", "at_site")$cost_all)` bits) but spill as much
again onto the following words
(`r f2(RC("wi", "function word", "spill")$cost_all)` bits). A missing article
or a wrong preposition is cheap where it occurs and costly for the words
after it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decay
#| fig-cap: "Mean spill onto an own word by its distance from the error, with 95% unit-bootstrap CIs"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
d <- dec |>
  mutate(corpus = factor(CORP[corpus], c("W&I", "FCE")),
         bucket = factor(bucket, c("all", BUCKETS)))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(d, mean_spill, colour = bucket)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~corpus) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = c(1:4, "5+")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(all = "black", mechanical = "#1b9e77", `function word` = "#d95f02",
                                 `content-word choice` = "#7570b3", `multi-word / order` = "#e7298a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Distance from the error (words)", y = "Mean spill per word (bits)") +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "spill_decay", 8, 3.4, dir = R3)
p
```

Spill falls off quickly with distance (Figure 2). Over all corrections it
roughly halves with each word, from
`r f2(filter(dec, corpus == "wi", bucket == "all", d == 1)$mean_spill)` bits on
the next word to `r f2(filter(dec, corpus == "wi", bucket == "all", d == 2)$mean_spill)`,
`r f2(filter(dec, corpus == "wi", bucket == "all", d == 3)$mean_spill)` and
`r f2(filter(dec, corpus == "wi", bucket == "all", d == 4)$mean_spill)` bits at
distances 2–4 (W&I; FCE is nearly identical). Multi-word and order
corrections spread the most, mechanical errors the least. The 8-subword
window cuts the reach at a few words, so the decay beyond that is partly the
window.

## 4.3 Association with proficiency

```{r}
#| label: t-split4-shares
s4 |>
  filter(part != "total") |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], measure = recode(measure, mean_surprisal = "mean surprisal", high_per_1000 = "high-token rate"),
            part = recode(part, error_tokens = "error tokens"),
            `share of the signal, % [95% CI]` = pci(share, lo, hi), `ρ with criterion` = ci2(rho, rho_lo, rho_hi)) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 5. Each part's share of the covariance of the essay measure with the criterion (CEFR level, script score), learners only")
```

All of the learner proficiency signal in mean surprisal lies in what the
corrections remove (Table 5). In W&I the clean part's share is
`r with(S4("wi", "clean"), pci(share, lo, hi))`% and its correlation with level
is `r f2(S4("wi", "clean")$rho)`. In FCE it is
`r with(S4("fce", "clean"), pci(share, lo, hi))`%, so the corrections carry
`r pc(1 - S4("fce", "clean")$share)`% of the FCE signal. The error tokens carry
the most (`r pc(S4("wi", "error_tokens")$share)`% and
`r pc(S4("fce", "error_tokens")$share)`%). About a quarter
(`r pc(S4("wi", "context")$share)`% and `r pc(S4("fce", "context")$share)`%) is
errors raising the surprisal of the correct words after them, and a tenth is
the word after a missing word. The high-token rate of Studies 1 and 2 splits
the same way, and on W&I its clean part runs against the total.

```{r}
#| label: t-bucket-shares
er <- sh |> filter(cut == "edit_rate")
sh |>
  filter(cut == "bucket", str_detect(col, "\\|") | col == "clean") |>
  separate(col, c("cat", "comp"), sep = "\\|", fill = "right") |>
  mutate(comp = replace_na(comp, "total"), v = pci(share, lo, hi)) |>
  select(corpus, cat, comp, v) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = comp, values_from = v) |>
  left_join(er |> transmute(corpus, cat = col, `share of edits` = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share_of_edits),
                            `share of the edit-rate signal` = pci(share, lo, hi)), by = c("corpus", "cat")) |>
  mutate(cat = factor(cat, c("clean", BUCKETS, "unclassified", "flagged", "residual"))) |>
  arrange(desc(corpus), cat) |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], component = cat, `at site` = at_site, spill, total,
            `share of edits`, `share of the edit-rate signal`) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(as.character(.x), ""))) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 6. Each component's share of the proficiency signal in mean surprisal, % [95% CI]. For comparison, each kind's share of all edits and of the covariance of the edit rate with the criterion")
```

By kind of correction (Table 6), mechanical corrections carry the largest
share, `r pc(SH("wi", "mechanical|total")$share)`% in W&I and
`r pc(SH("fce", "mechanical|total")$share)`% in FCE. Content-word choice and
multi-word or order corrections together carry
`r pc(SH("wi", "content-word choice|total")$share + SH("wi", "multi-word / order|total")$share)`%
and
`r pc(SH("fce", "content-word choice|total")$share + SH("fce", "multi-word / order|total")$share)`%,
and function words `r pc(SH("wi", "function word|total")$share)`% and
`r pc(SH("fce", "function word|total")$share)`%. These shares are close to each
kind's share of the edit-rate signal, the covariance of the plain error rate
with the criterion. Relative to the error counts, surprisal gives somewhat
more weight to multi-word corrections and less to function words, which
follows from their costs in Table 4. Spill is a fifth to a third of each
kind's share, and close to half for function words on W&I.

```{r}
#| label: t-rate-cost
rc |>
  filter(cut == "bucket", cat %in% BUCKETS, comp == "total") |>
  transmute(`kind of correction` = cat,
            `errors per 100 tokens, lowest → highest` = sprintf("%.1f → %.1f", if_else(corpus == "wi", rate_A, `rate_1-23`),
                                                               if_else(corpus == "wi", rate_C, `rate_32-40`)),
            `bits per error, lowest → highest` = sprintf("%.1f → %.1f", if_else(corpus == "wi", cost_A, `cost_1-23`),
                                                         if_else(corpus == "wi", cost_C, `cost_32-40`)),
            corpus = CORP[corpus],
            `share of the gap due to error rate, %` = pci(rate_share, rate_share_lo, rate_share_hi),
            `change in bits per error` = ci2(cost_change, cost_change_lo, cost_change_hi)) |>
  relocate(corpus) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 7. Frequency vs cost per error between the lowest and highest level (W&I A vs C; FCE score 1–23 vs 32–40)")
```

The components track proficiency mainly through how often the errors occur
(Table 7). The fall in error rate accounts for
`r pc(min(filter(rc, cut == "bucket", cat %in% BUCKETS, comp == "total")$rate_share))`–`r pc(max(filter(rc, cut == "bucket", cat %in% BUCKETS, comp == "total")$rate_share))`%
of the low-to-high difference for every kind of correction in both corpora.
The remainder is cost. In W&I, mechanical and multi-word errors cost about
`r sprintf("%.1f", -RC("wi", "mechanical")$cost_change)`–`r sprintf("%.1f", -RC("wi", "multi-word / order")$cost_change)`
bits less per error at C than at A, and content-word errors cost about the
same at every level. Spill per function-word error does not change with level
(`r with(RC("wi", "function word", "spill"), ci2(cost_change, cost_change_lo, cost_change_hi))`
bits in W&I).

```{r}
#| label: t-clean
ca |>
  filter(measure == "mean_surprisal") |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], statistic = recode(stat, rho_total = "ρ, mean surprisal", rho_clean = "ρ, clean part",
                                                     partial_clean = "partial ρ, clean part | share of corrected tokens"),
            value = ci2(value, lo, hi, 3)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = value) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 8. The clean part against the criterion, Spearman ρ [95% CI]")
```

The clean part's own association with proficiency is small and not
consistent across corpora (Table 8). In W&I it correlates slightly
positively with level, and more so at a given share of corrected tokens
(partial ρ `r with(filter(ca, corpus == "wi", measure == "mean_surprisal", stat == "partial_clean"), f2(value))`).
In FCE it correlates slightly negatively with the score, with or without the
control (partial ρ `r with(filter(ca, corpus == "fce", measure == "mean_surprisal", stat == "partial_clean"), f2(value))`).
The high-token rate shows the same sign difference. The surprisal of the
writer's corrected text is therefore not a stable proficiency signal of its
own. It mixes surprise that rises with level (vocabulary, register) with what
minimal corrections leave behind (awkward phrasing, missed errors), and the
balance differs between the corpora.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Supplement: the finer ERRANT groups

```{r}
#| label: t-groups
sh |>
  filter(cut == "group", str_detect(col, "\\|total$") | col == "clean") |>
  transmute(corpus, group = str_remove(col, "\\|total$"), v = pci(share, lo, hi)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = v) |>
  left_join(rc |> filter(cut == "group", comp == "total") |>
              transmute(corpus, group = cat, r = sprintf("%.1f / %.1f", rate_all, cost_all)) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = r, names_prefix = "rate / cost "), by = "group") |>
  transmute(group, `W&I share, %` = wi, `FCE share, %` = fce,
            `W&I errors per 100 tokens / bits per error` = `rate / cost wi`,
            `FCE errors per 100 tokens / bits per error` = `rate / cost fce`) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(.x, ""))) |>
  kable(caption = "Share of the proficiency signal by ERRANT group (at site + spill), and frequency and cost per error")
```
:::

## 4.4 Beyond error counts (RQ3)

```{r}
#| label: t-rq3
inc |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], model, units = format(n, big.mark = ","), `R²` = sprintf("%.3f", r2),
            `ΔR² over B [95% CI]` = if_else(is.na(delta_r2), "", ci2(delta_r2, lo, hi, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 9. Predicting level (W&I) and script score (FCE) from the error counts B and the surprisal components S (cross-validated R²)")
```

The human error counts alone explain most of what surprisal does (Table 9).
They reach R² = `r f2(INC("wi", "B")$r2)` on W&I and
`r f2(INC("fce", "B")$r2)` on FCE, against `r f2(INC("wi", "mean surprisal")$r2)`
and `r f2(INC("fce", "mean surprisal")$r2)` for mean surprisal alone. The
compact surprisal terms add a small but reliable increment on both corpora,
`r with(INC("wi", "B + S compact"), ci2(100 * delta_r2, 100 * lo, 100 * hi))`
points of R² on W&I and
`r with(INC("fce", "B + S compact"), ci2(100 * delta_r2, 100 * lo, 100 * hi))`
on FCE. Plain mean surprisal adds nothing on W&I and most of the gain on FCE.

```{r}
#| label: t-coefs
cf |>
  filter(model == "B + S compact", feature %in% c("clean", "cost_mean", "spill_mean")) |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], term = recode(feature, cost_mean = "mean at-site bits per error",
                                                 spill_mean = "mean spill bits per error"), coef_sd) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = coef_sd) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Table 10. Standardised ridge coefficients of the surprisal terms in B + S (criterion units per SD), all units")
```

The cost terms have the same sign in both corpora (Table 10). At a given
number of errors, errors that are more surprising, at their site and on the
words after them, go with a lower level or score. The clean term has opposite
signs in the two corpora, as in Table 8.

## 4.5 Follow-up (*post hoc*): classic measures under correction

This section was added after the results above had been seen. It asks
whether the dependence on correctable errors is specific to surprisal or is
shared by the phraseological and lexical measures of applied linguistics.

```{r}
#| label: t-classic
mlab <- c(surprisal = "mean surprisal", bigram_mi = "bigram MI", bigram_dp = "bigram ΔP", share_mi3 = "share of bigrams with MI ≥ 3",
          dep_mi = "dependency MI (amod, dobj, advmod)", content_freq = "content-word log frequency",
          lemma_freq = "Study 2 lemma log frequency")
cl |>
  filter(measure %in% names(mlab), stat %in% c("rho_orig", "rho_corr", "removed", "dR2_corr"),
         measure != "lemma_freq" | corpus == "fce") |>
  mutate(v = case_when(stat == "removed" ~ pci(value, lo, hi),
                       stat == "dR2_corr" ~ ci2(100 * value, 100 * lo, 100 * hi),
                       TRUE ~ ci2(value, lo, hi))) |>
  select(corpus, measure, stat, v) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = v) |>
  mutate(measure = factor(mlab[measure], mlab)) |>
  arrange(desc(corpus), measure) |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], measure, `ρ, original` = rho_orig, `ρ, corrected` = rho_corr,
            `removed by correction, %` = removed, `ΔR² over B, corrected essay (points)` = dR2_corr) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 11. Each measure against the criterion on the original and the corrected essays. Removed = 1 − ρ corrected / ρ original (for mean surprisal, 1 − the clean part's share). Study 2's lemma frequency has no association with level on W&I and is shown for FCE only")
```

Correction removes most of the proficiency association of the
phraseological measures too (Table 11). Bigram MI and the share of high-MI
bigrams lose nearly all of it on W&I
(`r pc(CL("wi", "bigram_mi", "removed")$value)`% and
`r pc(CL("wi", "share_mi3", "removed")$value)`%) and about half on FCE
(`r pc(CL("fce", "bigram_mi", "removed")$value)`% and
`r pc(CL("fce", "share_mi3", "removed")$value)`%). Dependency MI loses
`r pc(CL("wi", "dep_mi", "removed")$value)`% and
`r pc(CL("fce", "dep_mi", "removed")$value)`%. Bigram ΔP keeps most of its
association, and content-word frequency, a measure of lexical
sophistication, keeps all of it. On the corrected essays, only content-word
frequency adds to the error counts on both corpora. Bigram ΔP adds on W&I,
and its FCE interval touches zero.

```{r}
#| label: t-classic-buckets
cols <- c("corr", BUCKETS, "phraseological", "phraseological + function word")
cl |>
  filter(measure %in% names(mlab), str_starts(stat, "share\\|"), measure != "lemma_freq" | corpus == "fce") |>
  mutate(part = str_remove(stat, "share\\|")) |>
  filter(part %in% cols) |>
  mutate(v = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * value)) |>
  select(corpus, measure, part, v) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = part, values_from = v) |>
  bind_rows(sh |> filter(cut == "edit_rate", col %in% BUCKETS) |>
              select(corpus, col, share) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = share) |>
              mutate(phraseological = `content-word choice` + `multi-word / order`,
                     `phraseological + function word` = phraseological + `function word`,
                     across(-corpus, ~ sprintf("%.0f", 100 * .x)), measure = "edit_rate", corr = "–")) |>
  mutate(measure = factor(c(mlab, edit_rate = "reference: error rate")[measure], c(mlab, "reference: error rate"))) |>
  arrange(desc(corpus), measure) |>
  transmute(corpus = CORP[corpus], measure, corrected = corr, !!!syms(cols[-1])) |>
  kable(caption = "Table 12. Share of each measure's proficiency signal (%) carried by the corrected essay and by each kind of correction. Phraseological = content-word choice + multi-word / order")
```

Table 12 splits each measure's signal by kind of correction. Mean
surprisal's split follows the error mix, close to the reference row for the
plain error rate. Its narrowly phraseological part (content-word choice and
multi-word corrections) is
`r pc(CL("wi", "surprisal", "share|phraseological")$value)`% on W&I and
`r pc(CL("fce", "surprisal", "share|phraseological")$value)`% on FCE, and about
half with function words added. Bigram MI and the high-MI share also carry a
large mechanical part (`r pc(CL("wi", "bigram_mi", "share|mechanical")$value)`%
and `r pc(CL("wi", "share_mi3", "share|mechanical")$value)`% on W&I), because
misspellings and punctuation errors break bigrams. Dependency MI is the most
phraseological measure, led by content-word choice
(`r pc(CL("wi", "dep_mi", "share|content-word choice")$value)`% and
`r pc(CL("fce", "dep_mi", "share|content-word choice")$value)`%). On FCE,
Study 2's lemma frequency is a misspelling artifact. Its association with the
score is positive on the original scripts
(ρ = `r f2(CL("fce", "lemma_freq", "rho_orig")$value)`), mechanical corrections
carry `r pc(CL("fce", "lemma_freq", "share|mechanical")$value)`% of it, and it
turns negative after correction
(ρ = `r f2(CL("fce", "lemma_freq", "rho_corr")$value)`). Misspelled words are
unseen lemmas, which the measure counts at the frequency floor. On W&I the
measure has no association with level
(ρ = `r f2(CL("wi", "lemma_freq", "rho_orig")$value)`).

# 5. Discussion

**RQ1.** The surprisal of learner writing decomposes into a clean part and
the contributions of the errors, and the error part splits exactly by error
type. Each kind of error adds surprisal at its own site and spills onto the
next few words. Function-word errors are cheap at their site and spill the
most relative to it. Content-word and multi-word errors are the costliest per
error. Mechanical errors are the most frequent.

**RQ2.** Among learners, the proficiency signal in mean surprisal is the
errors. The corrections remove all of it on W&I and about nine tenths on FCE.
The components differ in how much of the signal they carry, but mostly
because the errors differ in frequency. Each component's share is close to
its share of the plain error-rate signal, and the fall in error rate explains
most of every component's difference between low and high levels. About a
quarter of the signal is spillover onto the correct words that follow an
error.

**RQ3.** Surprisal adds little to the human error counts. The increment is
reliable but small, and its consistent part is the cost of the errors, not
the clean text. Surprisal is better read as a model-based estimate of error
density, weighted by how disruptive the errors are, than as a measure of
something beyond errors.

Two consequences for the measure follow. First, lower mean surprisal is not
better writing above the C level. Native student essays sit at the C-learner
level, and more literate native prose is more surprising. The scale runs
from many errors to few, not from learner to native. Second, the
phraseological measures of applied linguistics share this dependence on
correctable errors. Bigram MI and the high-MI share lose most of their
association once errors are corrected, and a large part of what they lose is
spelling and punctuation. Study 2's lemma-frequency measure is, on FCE, an
index of misspelling. Studies that use these measures as indices of lexical
or phraseological knowledge should check how much of their signal survives
correction.

## Limitations

- **Minimal corrections.** The annotators corrected errors with as small an
  edit as possible. Awkward but grammatical phrasing is usually left alone
  and stays in the clean part, so the error components are a lower bound on
  what fluent rewriting would remove.
- **One annotator.** Only the first annotator's corrections are used.
  Annotators disagree on what counts as an error, and the split inherits that
  uncertainty.
- **The 8-subword window.** Spill is measured only within the window, so the
  spill shares are lower bounds, and its decay with distance is partly the
  window.
- **Dolma as reference.** The classic measures depend on the Dolma reference
  corpora (edited prose for the bigram measures), so their values reflect
  that corpus's register.
- **Untyped spans.** Flagged spans have no correction and no type
  (`r pc(SH("wi", "flagged|total")$share)`% of the W&I signal and
  `r pc(SH("fce", "flagged|total")$share)`% of the FCE signal).
- **Calibration.** PERSUADE's English-learner flag is a school category, not
  native-speaker status, and the calibration groups differ in topic, genre
  and age.
